subject: Chemistry
topic: Stability of higher oxidation states: oxides and fluorides
title: Fluorine Fails, Oxygen Wins: Highest Oxidation States in Oxides and Fluorides
summary: A metal reaches its highest oxidation state only with oxygen or fluorine. Fluorine is the more electronegative, yet manganese's highest fluoride is MnF₄ (+4) while its oxide reaches +7 (Mn₂O₇, MnO₄⁻): one oxygen forms a multiple bond and counts two electrons, one fluorine counts only one. From Sc₂O₃ to Mn₂O₇ the highest oxide's oxidation state equals the group number.

notes.title: 08 – Stability of Higher Oxidation States: Oxides and Fluorides

keyPoints: The **highest oxidation state** of a metal appears only in its **oxides and fluorides** (small, highly electronegative partners).
**Fluorine**: single bond, **1 electron per atom**; Mn's highest fluoride is **MnF₄ (+4)**, MnF₇ has never been made.
**Oxygen**: **multiple bond**, **2 electrons per atom**; only four O are needed: **MnO₄⁻** and **Mn₂O₇ (+7)**. Oxygen does not "pull harder".
**Highest oxide = group number**: Sc₂O₃ +3, TiO₂ +4, V₂O₅ +5, CrO₃ +6, Mn₂O₇ +7. A state this high is a **strong oxidising agent** (KMnO₄).

sections.h: Why oxygen goes further than fluorine

blocks.p: In MnO₄⁻, 4 × 2 = 8 electrons: 7 from Mn and 1 from potassium, hence the 1− charge (x + 4(−2) = −1, x = +7). The oxidation state is a counting rule; there is no free Mn⁷⁺ ion.

sections.h: Highest oxides of the 3d metals (NCERT Table 4.6)

blocks.p: Beyond Mn, no iron oxide above Fe₂O₃ is known. Mn₂O₇ is covalent: two MnO₄ tetrahedra sharing one oxygen.

sections.h: Highest fluorides and the Cu⁺ case

list: Highest halides: TiX₄ (+4), VF₅ (+5), CrF₆ (+6), MnF₄ (+4), FeX₃ and CoF₃ (+3). Mn reaches +7 with fluorine only in the oxofluoride MnO₃F.
Fluorine stabilises high states by high lattice energy (CoF₃) or high bond enthalpy (VF₅, CrF₆).
Cu⁺(aq) disproportionates: 2Cu⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Cu, because Cu²⁺'s much more negative hydration enthalpy outweighs the second ionisation enthalpy.
Cu²⁺ oxidises iodide: 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → Cu₂I₂ + I₂, so CuI₂ is not known.

quiz.explain: One O counts two electrons; F is the more electronegative.

simulation.reason: The idea is a counting rule (1 electron per F, 2 per O); the video, memory cards and notes teach it fully, and there is no variable a student would usefully change.
